entities.summary:
The Battle of Verdun was a pivotal event in the First World War, a 303-day battle that took place on the Western Front between German and French forces from February 21 to December 18, 1916. Located in Verdun, France, the battle was a brutal and devastating conflict that tested the limits of human endurance and the strength of the French army. The battle saw over 700,000 casualties, with 377,000 French soldiers killed or wounded, and 337,000 German soldiers killed or wounded. The battle was a turning point in the war, marking a shift in momentum in favor of the Allies.

The Battle of Verdun was a clash of industrialized warfare, with both sides employing massive artillery and machine gun fire. The battle saw the introduction of new tactics, including the use of trenches and the development of camouflage. The French army was led by General Philippe Pétain, who implemented a policy of attrition, wearing down the German army through sheer numbers and determination. The battle was a testament to the bravery and resilience of the soldiers who fought in it, and its legacy continues to be felt in modern-day France.

The Battle of Verdun had a profound impact on the course of the First World War and the development of modern warfare. The battle marked a shift in the balance of power on the Western Front, with the Allies gaining the upper hand. The battle also had a lasting impact on the French people, who continued to grapple with the trauma and loss of the battle for generations to come. In the years following the battle, the French government built numerous memorials and cemeteries to honor the soldiers who fought and died in the battle.

'Verdun will be reborn from its ashes.' - General Philippe Pétain
